headline: New adversarial pattern blocks surveillance cameras from detecting people and vehicles
summary: After 31 million tests, a computer-generated pattern can prevent common surveillance cameras and license plate readers from detecting objects and people it covers.
details: Bill Swearingen spent a year running 31 million tests to create a computer-generated pattern. This pattern, when applied to clothing or objects, prevents common surveillance cameras and license plate readers from detecting them. His project is called noRecognition.

The patterns do not block cameras from recording video footage. Instead, they scramble the camera's ability to identify objects, people, or faces, preventing detection alerts. This effectively makes the covered subject invisible to automated algorithmic surveillance.

Swearingen developed this to allow people to "opt-out of being tracked," citing privacy as a fundamental right. He was motivated by the pervasive surveillance in his town and concerns about tracking individuals exercising constitutional rights.

The pattern was successfully demonstrated in its first public test at the Def Con cybersecurity conference in Las Vegas. It proved effective at defeating surveillance detection when printed on a vehicle.

His research built on earlier work, evolving into a reinforcement learning model. This self-contained system trained itself to find effective patterns against specific camera algorithms, essentially teaching itself "how to paint" to evade detection.

headline_marked: [[Musk's Terafab projected to be larger than 100 million sq. ft]], dwarfing major landmarks combined
headline: Musk's Terafab projected to be larger than 100 million sq. ft, dwarfing major landmarks combined
summary: The all-in-one chip manufacturing facility is visualized to have a massive footprint, aiming to meet the 1TW compute needs of SpaceX and Tesla.
details: Elon Musk's Terafab project is visualized to be the largest interior structure on Earth, with a projected floor space of at least 100 million square feet. This massive facility aims to consolidate chip manufacturing processes.

To put its scale into perspective, Terafab is larger than Giga Texas (10 million sq. ft), the Pentagon (6.6 million sq. ft), Apple Park (2.82 million sq. ft), and the Mall of America (5.6 million sq. ft), all combined. It also significantly surpasses China's New Century Global Center, which has 18.9 million sq. ft.

The immense space is necessary as Terafab will be an all-in-one facility, producing logic and memory chips, and integrating lithography, packaging, and testing under one roof. This comprehensive approach is unusual for chip fabs.

Musk announced the project in March, driven by the need for at least 1TW of compute for SpaceX and Tesla, which exceeds the current global chip supply by over ten times. This self-sufficiency aims to secure critical AI processing power.

Industry leaders like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have called such a project "extremely hard," but Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan sees Musk as an ideal partner for "unconventional" manufacturing. Musk has a history of leading seemingly impossible ventures, from Tesla's EV revolution to SpaceX's commercial space travel.

Estimated to require up to $119 billion in investments, Terafab represents Musk's largest project to date. Despite a secure customer base in SpaceX and Tesla, the company acknowledges the ambitious megafactory carries inherent risks of success.
